Conversation fieldnotes

Your English • July 2 – August 10, 2026

Three small shifts.
More room for your ideas.

These patterns recur across different sessions. Each gives you a practical cue for telling a story, asking for help, or sharing information.

Start anywhere. Explore an example, try a short practice, or choose just one reminder to use next time.

01 / Finished events

Let the verb carry the time, too.

In the recorded examples, words such as “yesterday” place an event in the past, but the event verb stays in its base form. For these completed events, use the past simple.

From your record • excerpt

Yesterday I go to the market.

Correction

Yesterday I went to the market.

Your conversation cue

When you say “yesterday,” “last…” or “…ago,” check the verb that describes the finished event.

Past forms needed in these records:

go → wentbuy → boughtsee → sawmeet → mettake → tooksend → sent

You do not need to put every verb in the past. In the same source, “I remember that day clearly” describes remembering now, so “remember” can stay.

Try it • new learning example

A quick story about yesterday

“Yesterday I ___ a friend after work.”

Make it yours

Optional rehearsal only; your writing is not automatically checked or saved.

See a model and a self-check

New model: Yesterday I took a walk after dinner.

Find your event verb. Does its form match the finished time? Leave any statement about how you feel or what you remember now in the present if that is your meaning.

02 / Quantities

Keep the noun. Count the pieces.

Advice, information, furniture and equipment are uncountable in these everyday meanings. Use “some” or “a lot of” for an amount, and “pieces of” when the number matters.

From your record

She gave me two useful advices.

Correction

She gave me two useful pieces of advice.

Your conversation cue

Before adding “a,” a number, or a plural -s, ask: am I counting this noun, or individual pieces of it?

some advicea lot of informationthree pieces of furnituretwo pieces of equipment

Put the plural on pieces, not on advice. “An advice” needs a change too: say “some advice” or “a piece of advice.”

Does this apply to every noun?

No—meaning matters. Your original “I bought a coffee before the train” is fine when it means one cup. Keep that useful expression.

Source: M36-U04 • original accepted in context

Try it • new learning example

Ask for help with a decision

Which version fits ordinary conversation?

Make it yours

Optional rehearsal only; your writing is not automatically checked or saved.

See a model and a self-check

New model: Could you give me some information about the museum?

Check that “information” has no plural -s. For a specific number, you can use “two pieces of information.”

Trace the examples • 8 records, 8 sessions

03 / Embedded questions

Inside the question, use statement order.

After “Could you tell me…,” “Do you know…” or “I wonder…,” the question clause normally uses subject + verb order—not the order of a standalone question.

From your record

Could you tell me where is the station?

Correction

Could you tell me where the station is?

Your conversation cue

After the question word, name the person or thing first, then give its verb: where + the station + is.

New learning examples • direct → embedded

When does the café close?
Do you know when the café closes?

Why did he leave?
I wonder why he left.

Remove question-helper “do / does / did” from the inner clause. The main verb carries the form: “closes” or “left.” The outer “Do you know…” stays a question.

Try it • new learning example

Check a departure time

“Do you know ___?”

Make it yours

Optional rehearsal only; your writing is not automatically checked or saved.

See a model and a self-check

New model: Could you tell me where the library is?

Read the part after “where.” Does the subject come before “is”? You can use this same order after “I wonder…”

Trace the examples • 7 records, 7 sessions

About this selection

This report uses the supplied records from 40 sessions, not full transcripts. The three selected patterns are supported by examples across multiple sessions and are useful in everyday conversation.

The counts describe recorded examples and the distinct sessions containing them—not error rates. Repeated wording in separate sessions is counted as separate records; matching examples are grouped in the evidence views. Unchanged records do not tell us how often each structure was attempted.

Recurrence across sessions was given more weight than many similar examples in one session. Optional formal rewrites and proposals that would change an intended meaning or make a correct sentence incorrect were not treated as errors.

“From your record” identifies supplied wording. Corrections are shown separately. Practice prompts and models marked “new” were written for this report.

A small rehearsal is enough. You can leave whenever you like.
